newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Teva denies problems with Copaxone.
newsitem.headline: Teva denies problems with Copaxone.

text.p: Israel's Teva Pharmaceutical Industries said on Wednesday reports that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had ordered changes in the labelling of the company's Copaxone drug were unfounded.

"Already two months ago we scheduled the official launch of Copaxone for March 31, and so it will be. The product is already in distribution channels," chief financial officer Dan Seusskind told Reuters.

Copaxone is a proprietary treatment for multiple sclerosis (MS) that won FDA marketing clearance in December. Analysts expect the drug to produce peak revenues of $200-300 million annually. In 1996 Teva had revenues of $954 million.
Teva's Nasdaq share price fell 6.2 percent on Tuesday to 53 15/16, which Dillon, Read & Co in a report today attributed to the rumours.
Dillon said it traced the rumours to an equity report published by a rival brokerage on Biogen, a company with a competing MS treatment.
"The comments ... suggested that the removal of a line concerning the progression of MS from Copaxone's label has delayed the product's launch," Dillon said.
"In fact, the line had nothing to do with what Copaxone is indicated for ... nor how physicians prescribe the product. The line was actually take out six months ago," it added.
Dillon said the drop in Teva's share price from $64 in the last two weeks made the shares "extremely undervalued" as Teva is currently showing earnings per share of $0.50 a quarter.
"With the market placing such little value on Copaxone now, we believe this is a prime buying opportunity," Dillon said, assigning Teva a 12-18-month target price of $80.
